Online romance scams are among the oldest tricks in the online world, yet new victims continue to fall for them. A joint study by four universities has found that AI chatbots now outperform real people at these scams — a truly worrying development……

網上情緣騙案

Modern online romance scams typically start on dating apps. Scammers use a highly attractive profile to reach out to the victim, posing as an enthusiastic suitor who ticks every box on the victim's wish list.

They engage the victim in long online conversations, often stretching over several months. They excuse themselves by claiming to be on an extended trip abroad, which is why they can't meet up in the short term.

Eventually, one of two things usually happens: either they claim to have hit some sudden emergency and need an immediate wire transfer to get out of trouble, or they steer the conversation towards their supposedly successful investment track record, persuading the victim to pour money into a fake cryptocurrency scheme.

These scams are called "long cons" precisely because the scammer needs time — often chatting daily for months — to build trust. Although it looks labour-intensive, these operations are usually run out of scam compounds in places like Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos, carried out by extremely low-paid workers — some of whom are trafficking victims forced to do the job.

AI versus humans

Wired magazine reported on a study carried out jointly by four universities, using ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini in the process.

Researchers from four universities — Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham in India, Foscari University in Venice, the University of Melbourne, and Ben-Gurion University of the Negev — pitted AI chatbots directly against real people, simulating the entire scam process; more precisely, simulating that lengthy trust-building conversation that eventually lures the target into investing in a bogus project. They found that……the AI chatbots performed remarkably well, successfully impersonating humans, and on some metrics even outperformed the human "scammers" in the experiment.

The subjects did not know the true purpose of the study, and regardless of whether they were talking to a real person or not, they believed they were chatting with a real human. The researchers used both subjective and objective tests to measure the level of trust built up. When it came to the final stage — asking the subject to do something like downloading an app — only 18% of the group whose rapport had been cultivated by a real person agreed, while nearly half of those who had been talking to an AI chatbot agreed.

Furthermore, when subjects were asked to rate the level of trust they felt towards the "person" they had been chatting with, the AI bots scored significantly higher.

This technology could supercharge scam operations

Perhaps the most worrying finding of the study is that replacing human scammers with AI chatbots could allow scam centres to massively scale up their operations. A single AI scam bot could be holding conversations with thousands of victims simultaneously.

A human operator would only need to step in at the very last stage — when the money is actually being requested — in order to circumvent the safety guardrails built into AI systems.
